hints.S56_A1: The clouds STRETCHED IN EVERY DIRECTION WITHOUT END, and they are measured against an OCEAN. Ask: does the missing word describe size, or light, or width? 'Narrow' and 'small' would shrink the sky instead of opening it up.
hints.S56_A2: The delay SURPRISED ALL THE PASSENGERS - nobody saw it coming. Ask: which idiom means 'with no warning at all'? 'Little by little' is gradual, 'on purpose' is deliberate, and 'very slowly' is no surprise to anyone.
hints.S56_A3: The PLANE is leaving the ground and rising INTO THE BRIGHT AFTERNOON SKY. Ask: which phrasal verb means to leave the runway and begin flying? 'Land' brings it down, 'sink' pulls it under, and 'stop' halts it.
hints.S56_A4: You SHOW it at the GATE, and without it you cannot get ONTO THE PLANE. Ask: which choice is a document that names your flight and your seat? A suitcase is luggage, a photo is a picture, and a guide is a book.
hints.S56_A5: The dash explains it: PATIENCE and PROFESSIONALISM with a NERVOUS passenger. Ask: which word keeps the same positive direction as 'calm'? 'Rude', 'clumsy' and 'distracted' all point the opposite way.
hints.S56_B1: The subject is EVERYONE, not the crowd ON BOARD. Words like everyone and nobody behave like ONE person. Ask: in the present tense, does a singular subject take the plain verb, or the one ending in -s?
hints.S56_B2: HAS is already sitting there, so the blank must partner it. Ask: after 'has', do we use the plain verb, the -s form, the -ing form, or the past participle? This verb is irregular, so it never takes -ed.
hints.S56_B3: THAN tells you that exactly two terminals are being measured against each other, and the adjective is short. Ask: does a short adjective add -er, or take 'more' in front of it? And may you ever use both at once?
hints.S56_B4: The ALARM WENT OFF suddenly and cut across something already happening. Ask: which choice shows an action still in progress in the PAST? A plain past verb would only report a finished action.
hints.S56_B5: Read the second half: the airline is FULLY BOOKED, so the number of free seats is zero. Ask: which choice means 'not even one'? 'Little' and 'a little' belong to uncountable things, and 'much' cannot count seats.
hints.S56_B6: The statement is positive and its verb DISAPPOINTED is a plain past verb - there is no 'is' or 'was' to echo. Ask: which helping verb stands in for a past verb, and does a positive statement take a positive tag or a negative one?
hints.S56_B7: The LUGGAGE cannot check its own size: the staff do that, and it happened BEFORE BOARDING. Ask: which choice is passive (the subject receives the action) and set in the past? Luggage is uncountable, so treat it as one thing.
hints.S56_B8: ASKED THE PASSENGERS = a reported request. Ask: after 'asked + person', which form follows - the plain verb, the -ing form, or 'to' + verb? Only one of the four choices is a full infinitive.
hints.S56_C1: 'SINGLE PASSENGER' is one person at a time, and the rule holds WITHOUT EXCEPTION. Ask: which box word goes in front of a singular noun to mean 'all of them, nobody left out'? Its rival is needed for the pair of pilots.
hints.S56_C2: Look at what follows the blank: 'OF THE TWO PILOTS'. Ask: which box word can stand in front of 'of the ...' and pick the pilots out ONE BY ONE? Its rival can never be followed by 'of'.
hints.S56_C3: The blank sits in front of the plural noun PASSENGERS, and the rule covers everyone FROM THE YOUNGEST CHILD TO THE OLDEST ADULT. Ask: which box word takes a plural noun and leaves nobody out? 'Most' would let some stay unbuckled.
hints.S56_C4: Read to the end: A FEW STILL RUSH IN AT THE LAST MINUTE, so not every traveller is early. Ask: which box word means 'more than half, but not the whole group'? 'All' would contradict the second half of the sentence.
hints.S56_C5: The blank comes straight after 'is', with no noun behind it, and THIRTY MINUTES IS BARELY the amount needed. Ask: which box word means 'just as much as is needed, and no more'? A box phrase ending in 'of' cannot sit here.
hints.S56_C6: The dash explains the amount: FAR MORE CHAIRS THAN IT EVER NEEDS. Ask: which box phrase means a large amount, more than is needed? A word meaning 'just as much as is needed' would clash with 'far more'.
hints.S56_C7: The blank leads straight into the noun FOOD, and SNACKS MUST BE THROWN AWAY, so the amount is zero. Ask: which box word is an adjective that can touch a noun? 'None' is a pronoun and stands alone.
hints.S56_C8: The blank is followed by 'OF THE BAGS', so it stands on its own instead of leading into a noun. Ask: which box word is a pronoun meaning 'not a single one of them'? The adjective form can never be followed by 'of'.
hints.S56_D1: Travellers CHECK IN there and DROP OFF THEIR LUGGAGE, right at the start of the journey. Ask: which box word names the act of LEAVING on a flight? The runway, the cockpit and the height all come later.
hints.S56_D2: The clue sits in the same sentence: THE LONG FLAT STRIP WHERE AIRCRAFT TAKE OFF AND LAND. Ask: which box word names that strip of ground? It is the road planes drive along before they leave the earth.
hints.S56_D3: PILOTS SIT there, AT THE FRONT, SURROUNDED BY CONTROLS AND SCREENS. Ask: which box word names the small cabin from which the crew flies the plane? Passengers are never allowed inside it.
hints.S56_D4: The clue is the measurement: ABOUT TEN THOUSAND METRES ABOVE SEA LEVEL. The plane CLIMBS to it, so it must be a distance upwards. Ask: which box word names a height rather than a place or a movement?
hints.S56_D5: The dash explains it: SUDDEN CHANGES IN AIR MOVEMENT THAT ROCK THE AIRCRAFT, and passengers FEEL BUMPS. Ask: which box word names rough, shaking air? A runway or a cockpit cannot shake a plane in mid-air.
hints.S56_E1: Find the subject of the underlined verb: THE PASSENGERS - more than one person. Ask: does a plural subject take the singular past form, or the plural one? Match the verb to its subject, never to the word beside it.
hints.S56_E2: 'WHOSE' asks 'belonging to whom', but the boy only wants to know WHICH PERSON is flying the plane today. Ask: can the underlined word be stretched back into two full words, one of them a verb? An apostrophe hides a missing letter.
hints.S56_E3: 'RELEIF' has the E and the I the wrong way round. Ask: which of the two letters really comes first in this word? Remember the rule - I before E, except after C - the same order as in field, chief and piece.
hints.S56_E4: The underlined word tells us HOW the plane LANDED - it describes the action, not the plane. Ask: after an action verb, do we need an adjective or an adverb? An adverb of manner usually wears a two-letter tail.
hints.S56_E5: The VOICES belong to the PILOTS - more than one pilot owns them. Ask: does a plain -s show ownership, or only 'more than one'? When the owners are plural and already end in -s, where must the apostrophe stand?
hints.S56_F1: 'UNLESS' already means 'if not', so the negative is built into the word itself. Ask: should you keep the word 'not' from the first sentence, and may a future 'will' ever follow 'unless'? Sentence A gives the condition, B the result.
hints.S56_F2: Sentence B is still a question - 'WHAT IS THE DEPARTURE TIME FOR FLIGHT SQ317?' - but a reported sentence is not. Ask: after 'asked', does the subject come before the verb or after it? And which tense does a present verb slide into?
